title: Benchmark methodology workshop: runtime, KV cache, quant & VPC
summary: Deep dive on benchmark methodology for apples-to-apples comparisons across hosted, dedicated and on-prem deployments. Covered prompt set design, load generation patterns, warm-up and steady-state measurements, KV cache priming, batching strategies, quantization impact on latency and quality, and VPC/on-prem environment differences. Agreed next steps to run controlled pilot with shared harness and baseline prompts.
topics: KV cache priming and stateful conversations
action_items: Alex Chen (Redwood SE) - share benchmark harness repo and runbook - due 2025-12-15
Priya Kapoor (Nimbus AI) - provide representative prompt sets and traffic distribution CSV - due 2025-12-17
Daniel Ortiz (Nimbus AI) - provide VPC network diagram and access window for on-prem pilot - due 2025-12-18

Customer to share prompt sets and target SLOs for latency and cost

transcript: Meeting header: 2025-12-10 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~75 mins | Attendees: Samir, Alex, Priya, Daniel, Maya

14:00:02 - Samir (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. The goal today is to walk through a reproducible benchmark methodology so we can do apples-to-apples comparisons across Hosted, Dedicated and your on-prem infra.

14:00:18 - Priya (Head of ML): Thanks Samir. We're mainly worried about p95/p99 latency spikes and cost per token; we also need to understand how the KV cache behavior will change when we move to a stateful convo setup.

14:00:40 - Alex (SE): Totally. We'll cover prompt set curation, load generation patterns, warm up, steady-state, metrics to capture, and how to prime the KV cache. Quick note: some transcripts auto-mangle 'KV cache' to 'KV cash' so apologies if that shows up later in the raw logs.
14:01:05 - Daniel (Infra): For on-prem we have network egress rules, and we need to validate VPC peering latency too — that will affect measured tail latencies.
14:01:22 - Maya (ML Eng): Also want to see quantization effects on quality. We can tolerate small drop in F1 on our NER tasks but not hallucinations in prompt completion.
14:01:40 - Samir: Great, so first section — prompt sets. Alex, can you run through what a representative prompt set looks like for a benchmark?

14:01:54 - Alex: Sure. The idea is to create stratified buckets: short instructions (<=32 tokens), mid-length (32-128), long/contextual (128-1024). Include corner cases: token-heavy inputs, high-variance outputs, multi-turn dialogues to test KV cache. We recommend capturing a distribution file that lists request_type, mean_length, variance, and expected tokens out. Example: 'support-short, 12, 8, 64'.
14:02:30 - Priya: Do you recommend synthetic amplification or only real production prompts?

14:02:37 - Alex: Mix. Use real prompts as the baseline then amplify with paraphrases to stress the runtime without introducing unnatural lexical patterns. Paraphrasing should preserve semantic intent so quality checks remain representative.

14:03:05 - Samir: Next, load generation. We usually use k6 for HTTP and a thin tokeniser shim so token accounting matches the runtime. Important: control concurrency vs arrivals — do you model Poisson arrivals or fixed concurrency?

14:03:25 - Alex: For latency-sensitive systems model a Poisson or real-sess trace to capture spikes. For sustained throughput tests use fixed concurrency to measure max tokens/sec. Always run both: spike/arrival profile for SLOs, fixed concurrency for capacity planning.
14:04:10 - Daniel: How do you handle batching determinism? Our infra sometimes aggregates requests differently at high concurrency and that changes latency distributions.

14:04:22 - Alex: We tie batching strategies to both batch size and batch latency windows. For apples-to-apples, fix the max_batch_size and max_wait_ms in the runtime config across environments. Also capture the actual batch sizes observed in logs — that way you can normalize throughput by effective batch size.
14:04:58 - Maya: On KV cache — when you say priming, do you mean pre-warming the KV cache with typical conversation prefixes?

14:05:08 - Alex: Exactly. Priming means running a representative set of conversation turns to populate the KV cache so subsequent calls have cached KV keys. Compare cold-start runs (cache empty) vs warmed runs. For stateful apps, measure per-turn latency as the cache grows and with cache hits/misses ratio.
14:05:38 - Priya: What about multi-tenant noise on Dedicated? If other tenants spike, will that affect our p99?

14:05:49 - Samir: For Dedicated we provide isolated GPU pools, but for Hosted you need to test under realistic noisy neighbors. We recommend running a 'background noise' profile during hosted tests that simulates other customers' load to see the worst-case tails.
14:06:20 - Alex: Also capture hardware-level counters where possible — GPU util, memory pressure, kernel stalls. Those help correlate p99 spikes to resource saturation.
14:06:45 - Daniel: On VPC and on-prem, network serialization and TLS handshake times add to cold-start latency. Any recommended instrumentation?

14:06:55 - Alex: Instrument at three layers: client-side request timing (total RTT), gateway/proxy timing (ingress/egress), and model runtime. If you can expose socket-level metrics that helps isolate network vs runtime. For TLS, measure handshake rtt separately in baseline tests.
14:07:30 - Maya: Quantization — we want to test INT8 and FP16. How do you measure quality regressions systematically?

14:07:43 - Alex: Create a small but representative eval set (gold labels) per task. Compute automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/F1) plus a human spot-check sample. For open-gen prompts, use a reference-based metric where possible and include 'acceptability' buckets run by annotators. Track mismatch rates per prompt bucket.
14:08:10 - Priya: Any tips to avoid conflating quantization noise with prompt drift?

14:08:20 - Alex: Keep prompt sets fixed across runs and seed RNGs where possible. Run the same prompts on baseline FP16 and quantized models with identical model checkpoints (same architecture, same weights pre-quantization). Also run multiple seeds to estimate variance.

14:08:52 - Samir: Metrics to report: p50/p95/p99 latency, tail latency (99.9 if possible), tokens/sec (throughput), successful responses %, per-token cost estimate, batch-size distribution, KV cache hit ratio, and quality metrics per bucket.
14:09:20 - Daniel: For per-token cost estimate, do you provide standard accounting? We want something we can plug into financial models.

14:09:30 - Samir: We output micro-metrics: tokens_generated, tokens_consumed, GPU_time_ms, and convert GPU_time to cost using either cloud list prices or your Dedicated reserved rate. We can provide a calculator sheet.
14:09:55 - Maya: On apples-to-apples: what are the common gotchas you've seen?

14:10:03 - Alex: Main ones: different tokenizer behavior (token counts differ), different model weights/compilation flags, inconsistent batch configs, ignoring warm-up, and mismatched request timeouts. Also some environments squeeze for throughput with aggressive kernel fusions — that can change quality subtly if quantization paths differ.
14:10:40 - Priya: About tokenizer differences — do you recommend shipping a canonical tokenizer in the harness?

14:10:48 - Alex: Yes. Use the exact tokenizer binary or pip package used by the model. We provide a thin wrapper in the harness so token accounting is identical across runs. Link to sample harness: https://redwood-internal.example/bench/harness (private).

14:11:10 - Samir: Let's talk about experiment lifecycle: baseline, tuning, regression checks. Baseline: run cold-start and warmed steady-state. Tuning: vary batch size and quantization settings. Regression: after any model or infra change, re-run a small core set of prompts as a canary.
14:11:40 - Maya: For canary, how big is large enough? We have thousands of prompts but can't re-run all of them on every deploy.
14:11:50 - Alex: Start with a 200-500 prompt core set that covers all buckets and known failure modes. Use that to gate rollouts; if a canary fails, dive into the full set.
14:12:10 - Daniel: Can you run this harness within our VPC for on-prem tests? We have restrictions on outbound traffic.

14:12:20 - Samir: Yes. We can provide a private-runner that you deploy in your VPC; it streams metrics back over a secure channel or writes to S3-compatible storage if you prefer pulling artifacts. We'll coordinate with Daniel on access windows.
14:12:47 - Priya: Security and compliance — we need to ensure the harness doesn't persist PII. Can the runbook scrub inputs and store only hashes?
14:12:56 - Alex: Absolutely. The harness has options to hash or redact inputs and to redact outputs before persistent storage. We'll include that in the runbook and in the private deployment package.

14:13:25 - Samir: Quick detour — measuring cost at scale: include amortized model loading time across sessions and measure cold-start frequency under your expected traffic patterns. It's easy to undercount cold-starts if you only run long-lived concurrency tests.
14:13:52 - Maya: Good point. We'll share our session idle timeout patterns so you can model it.

14:14:05 - Alex: Finally, about result reproducibility: commit the harness version, seed, model checksum, and runtime flags as metadata with every run. We output a run manifest JSON (hash) — makes post-mortem comparisons easier.
14:14:30 - Priya: Next steps recap please?

14:14:35 - Samir: Sure. Alex will share the harness and runbook. Priya and team will share prompt sets and the target SLO spreadsheet. Daniel will provide VPC/network details and an access window. We'll schedule a 2-hour pilot next week to run Hosted vs Dedicated baselines and then an on-prem run.
14:14:55 - Alex: Action items noted. I'll also include a sample Jupyter notebook that parses logs and computes p50/p95/p99 and cost per token breakdown.
14:15:10 - Priya: Thank you, this was super helpful. Looking forward to the harness.
14:15:20 - Samir: Thanks everyone; we'll follow up with links and calendar invites. End call.
